title: The senseless cycle of Naga–Kuki violence in Manipur
author: Greeshma Kuthar
image_caption: NSCN(I–M) cadre stand guard in front of a mural of the Naga flag in Ukhrul.ANUPAM NATH / AP PHOTO
content_html:
{ONE}

VUMTHANG SITLHOU WAS in good spirits on the morning of 13 May. After an early breakfast and prayers, the 75-year-old Baptist priest had set out from the town of Churachandpur, in southern Manipur, to Kangpokpi, around a hundred kilometres to the north. The journey would have ordinarily taken around three hours, but, ever since the ethnic conflict between Kukis and Meiteis broke out three years earlier, the Imphal Valley has been off limits to members of the Kuki communities who inhabit the surrounding mountains, the largest of which is Vumthang’s Thadou tribe.

Despite four hundred thousand people facing severe restrictions in mobility, the state government has not created any alternative routes. Instead, residents of the hill districts have had to pool funds for makeshift roads constructed by various insurgent groups. Vumthang’s entourage—which included five other priests from the Thadou Baptist Association India, travelling in two SUVs marked with TBAI insignia—had to follow a circuitous route, various sections of which are called Tiger Road and German Road, after the noms de guerre of two militants of the Kuki National Front (President). While the Assam Rifles maintain a checkpoint before the road enters Kangpokpi, the route is largely controlled by groups such as the KNF(P) and the Kuki Revolutionary Army, which charge tolls for passage and security. Much of it is made up of mud roads that are impassable during the rains. Commuters travel in groups and are allowed to use the roads only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.

On that Wednesday morning, Goumang Lhouvum, who had become a close confidant of Vumthang while driving him across the Northeast over the past five years, hoped to make it to Kangpokpi before nightfall. He had queued up the priest’s favourite gospel songs to make the tumultuous journey less taxing. They reached Jouzangtek, a village in the Noney district, at 8 am and halted there for around forty-five minutes. Once they left, the others in the car dozed off, but Vumthang sat in the passenger seat, humming along to the music.

title: Fixing NEET fixes nothing, abolishing it does
author: Sujatha Sivagnanam
image_caption: A protester in Chennai carries a poster with a photo of S Anitha, who became the face of Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET. The exam severely accentuates inequalities in medical education.M Boomika, People’s Photographers Collective forThe Caravan
content_html:
S MANIRATHINAM was intent on continuing the struggle. “We will not quit this fight,” he told the hundreds of protesters gathered at Balan Illam, the Communist Party of India’s headquarters in Chennai. It was 25 July, and two thousand kilometres away, in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, the Cockroach Janta Party had called off the wide-scale protests that had swelled for days, up until the resignation of the union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. “We will continue to demand a ban on NEET,” Manirathinam said, referring to the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test, a centralised test introduced in 2017 amidst confusion and opposition. “Let us regroup. Let us continue our protest in a public place with government approval.” A lot of the protesters, however, were disappointed. They had wanted to continue the agitation. Manirathinam himself had spoken from the Jantar Mantar stage just days before and had seen the police beating protesters as they marched towards parliament. For him, and the agitation he returned to in Chennai, the demand was not merely to reform NEET, but to ban it.

The moment carried the weight of a nearly decade-long heartbreaking battle for Manirathinam. His sister, S Anitha, had died by suicide nine years ago, and her image had become a rallying point for Tamil Nadu’s anti-NEET movement. Since then, he had opposed the examination tooth and nail. He had organised petitions, fought legal battles, joined protests and even built a library in his sister’s memory. The Jantar Mantar protest had felt like a turning point: after years of fighting in Tamil Nadu, tens of thousands had finally gathered in the national capital to demand, among other things, accountability over NEET.

But when the protest was called off, the disappointment was palpable. It felt as though the anger that had briefly found a national stage suddenly had nowhere to go. Besides, it was clear to Manirathinam that the resignation of one minister could not settle the question. It could not undo the problems built into the examination, the system around it and the havoc it played on the lives of innumerable students. He believed the examination had deepened inequality in medical admissions and created impossible hurdles for students from rural areas. Nothing less than its rollback would work. The crowd at Balan Illam erupted, shouting, “Ban NEET!”

title: How the imperial myth of AI’s inevitability fuels resource extraction
author: Ajeet Mahale
content_html:
The term “artificial intelligence” has become ubiquitous in recent years, with supporters of the industry pointing to its seeming inevitability within the arc of technological progress. However, increasing evidence of the toll the industry is taking on the environment has prompted critics to argue that it is just another way for large corporations to control natural resources. CEOs of AI companies, often in public feuds with each other, have revealed their ambition to shape public ideas and infrastructures. These companies are in a race to consolidate power, militarise the industry and make themselves too big to fail.

The extent of the AI industry’s willingness to sideline fundamental ethical concerns in the pursuit of profit was on display during the US–Israel war on Iran, which started on 28 February. Among other targets, the United States bombed the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Minab, in Iran, and killed nearly one hundred and eighty people, most of them girls between the ages of seven and twelve. Anthropic, the company behind the AI model Claude, was reportedly linked to the bombing. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, later said he did not know how Claude had been used. He argued that its use had not violated the company’s red lines and that a human, not Claude, made the final call.

Karen Hao is a journalist and author who has written extensively on artificial intelligence. Her book Empire of AI profiled OpenAI and traced the rise of the industry. She also co-created the Pulitzer Center’s AI Spotlight Series, a programme that trains journalists on how to cover AI, and The AI Resist List, a project that counters Silicon Valley’s inevitability narrative by showcasing global grassroots movements holding the industry accountable. Ajeet Mahale, an assistant editor at The Caravan, spoke to her about the industry’s trajectory, the many contentious claims made by its supporters, and the more conscionable attempts to harness AI, which respect the environment and the dignity of local communities.

In India, we got a glimpse of the Sam Altman–Dario Amodei feud when they refused to hold hands during the AI summit. Your book describes cults of personalities in the industry. Has it always been like this?

title: The aftermath of the Muzaffarnagar riots
author: Joe Sacco
content_html: The journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot pieces together accounts of the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, which left 62 dead, and over fifty thousand displaced, the majority of whom were Muslim. In this excerpt from the book, published with permission from LeftWord Books, Sacco speaks to survivors of the violence, including those from the Muzaffarnagar and Shamli districts who were living in the displacement camps he visited. Muslim villagers recount the riot’s long-lasting after-effects, their efforts to get compensation, and the fear of returning to their villages.

title: A personal archive of longing across lost cities
image_caption: During a 2001 trip to India, Qamar took this self-portrait inside a family home in Kolkata, which was part of a guided city tour conducted by an Englishman. The house, she recalled, belonged to “an aristocratic family” and, though not very big, had ornate architecture, furniture, checkered floor tiles, and “a very Bengali essence to it.”
content_html:
I SAT ACROSS THE ROOM from Qamar Bharoocha Bana in her sea-facing apartment in Clifton, an upscale seaside locality of Karachi. The December sky was a soft amber with the evening fast setting in. She was quiet, turning a stack of photographs over in her hands as she settled into her canvas director’s chair beside the window overlooking the sea. Down at the beach, people moved in pairs and small groups, kids trailing behind or running ahead. It was a while before she spoke. “I most certainly miss Bombay, although I have a strong feeling that now it’s not the same Bombay that it was when I was growing up. I could feel the change happening all around me when I visited the last time in 2005,” she told me.

Through the winter of 2025, we were going through her archive—West Africa one week, Nepal the next, China after that. That day, it was India. “It’s a shame that I don’t have a lot of photographs from my last trip. You see, I had this uneasy feeling that I was constantly being watched and followed wherever I went. That discomfort was enough of a reason for me not to enjoy the time that I spent there on my last trip.”

This was a far cry from her visit in 2001, when she spent nearly six months travelling across the country, including Kolkata, Varanasi, Rajasthan, Mumbai and Delhi. “I was invited to a close friend’s son’s wedding in Delhi,” she said, and had travelled with her family from Karachi for the event. She said that after the wedding she stayed back “to chase my dreams of making photos of India.” She said she was particularly satisfied with the body of work she made during the trip, with her photos serving as an important record of places and moments that have since changed or disappeared.

title: Mohan Bhagwat brings a resurgent Sangh to the cusp of political power
author: Dinesh Narayanan
image_caption: Mohd Zakir / Hindustan Times / Getty Images
content_html:
|ONE|

IN EARLY AUGUST LAST YEAR, a cohort of journalists gathered in Kolkata for a two-day seminar on Islamic fundamentalism convened by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the world’s largest non-political voluntary organisation and the eighty-eight-year-old bedrock of Hindu nationalism in India. This was the first time the RSS, also known as the Sangh, had held such a workshop—one in a series of four, aimed specifically at journalists, on issues of significance to the organisation, including politics in Jammu and Kashmir, scheduled castes, and development. Only ideological devotees were allowed in. According to the RSS’s annual report, the four events—the others were in Delhi, Bangalore, and Ahmedabad—drew 220 participants from across the country.

In Kolkata, the RSS’s prachar pramukh, or head of promotion, and the chief organiser of the event, Manmohan Vaidya, laid out the objective: to help journalists understand the nuances of the RSS’s position so they could better project the Hindu nationalist point of view. The participants were instructed that the seminar was not to be reported on, or talked about outside RSS circles. “During some sessions, we were asked to let it go in one ear and out the other,” a journalist and swayamsevak, or RSS volunteer, who works for a regional newspaper, told me.

At one point, Shrirang Godbole, an endocrinologist from Maharashtra who serves as an Islam pundit within the Sangh, explained that the Muslim community is not monolithic, but is riven by divisions just like Hindus are by caste. He then expounded on how even “benign” sects such as Sufism have a violent past. “Some of our leaders pay homage to Sufi saints without proper understanding of history,” Godbole told them, as a slide showing the BJP leader LK Advani at the dargah in Ajmer, Rajasthan, popped up on a screen. The swayamsevak-journalist said it generated a lot of laughter—even from Mohan Bhagwat, the RSS sarsanghchalak, or supreme commander, who was present throughout the workshop.
